analysis.one_liner: Blocks apps and data brokers from collecting or selling people's reproductive and sexual health information.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2025 with 22 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and has had no hearings, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar companies outside the traditional health care system — period-tracking apps, fertility apps, search engines, and data brokers — from collecting, keeping, or selling personal reproductive and sexual health information unless it is strictly necessary to deliver a service the person asked for. It would give people the right to see what data a company holds about them, find out who it was sold to, correct it, and delete it, with a 15-day deadline and no fees. The Federal Trade Commission could enforce the rules, and individuals could sue for $100 to $1,000 per violation per day, with pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers unenforceable for these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose app, search, location, or purchase history could reveal reproductive health details: people seeking abortions or contraception, people using period- or fertility-tracking apps, people researching sexual health. Post-Dobbs, such data can be bought by others and used to infer where someone sought or obtained an abortion. The bill would cut off the collection and sale of that data at the source, give people access and deletion rights, and let them enforce the rules in court with damages that scale per day of violation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of health and period-tracking apps

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits regulated entities from collecting, retaining, using, or disclosing personal reproductive or sexual health information except as strictly necessary to provide a product or service the user requested, and restricts employee access to that data.

Gives individuals enforceable rights to access their data — including a list of the specific third parties it was disclosed to and data inferred about them — and to correct or delete it, which companies must honor within 15 days at no charge.

Covers not just obvious health records but inferred and algorithmic data, including location information that might indicate someone tried to obtain reproductive health services, contraceptive purchases, and even basal temperature or hormone data from wearables.

Creates FTC enforcement as an unfair or deceptive practice, plus a private right of action with statutory damages of $100 to $1,000 per violation per day, punitive damages, and attorney's fees — and voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for these disputes, so companies cannot force claims into individual arbitration.
Prohibits retaliation — denying service, charging different prices, or degrading service quality — against people who exercise their rights under the bill.

analysis.who_pays: Companies in the consumer data economy — data brokers, ad tech firms, app developers, and platforms — would bear compliance costs and lose the ability to monetize reproductive and sexual health data, including inferred data derived from browsing, location, and purchase history. They would also face litigation exposure from the private right of action and the removal of arbitration shields.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad tech, and app developers

drawbacks.text: The definition of covered data is broad — it reaches location information that 'might indicate' an attempt to acquire reproductive services and any data 'derived or extrapolated' from non-health information — which could sweep in ordinary browsing and location data and impose significant compliance costs, especially on small app developers.

The combination of statutory damages of $100–$1,000 per violation per day, punitive damages, attorney's fees, and a ban on pre-dispute arbitration and class-action waivers creates substantial litigation exposure that an honest supporter would acknowledge as a real cost to businesses and potentially to consumers through prices.

The bill excludes HIPAA-covered entities and their business associates, so doctors, hospitals, and insurers stay under existing medical-privacy rules rather than gaining the new rights; it addresses the app-and-broker layer, not the medical system itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protection is meaningful and the costs are real but narrow. After the Dobbs decision, reproductive health data held by non-medical companies can be used to infer who sought or obtained an abortion, which is a concrete risk to people; the bill cuts off collection and sale at the source and gives individuals usable enforcement tools. The main costs — compliance burden from a broad data definition and litigation exposure from per-day statutory damages without arbitration shields — fall on the data industry, though some could pass through to consumers as higher app prices or fewer features. On balance the benefits to ordinary people outweigh the costs, and the strongest good-faith objection is about the breadth of the covered-data definition rather than the goal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on June 11, 2025, and has sat there with no hearings, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Senator Mazie Hirono introduced the My Body, My Data Act of 2025 on June 11, 2025, joined on introduction by 19 other Democratic senators including Wyden, Blumenthal, Klobuchar, and Cantwell.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

The cosponsor list grew to 22 senators, all Democrats, but the action history shows nothing after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — while Congress remains in session through January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, ad tech firms, and app makers are better off so far: with the bill stalled in committee, they can continue collecting and selling reproductive and sexual health data under current rules, and no one has gained the privacy protections it would create.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and ad tech, for now

for.name: Sen. Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 11, 2025 and shepherded it to referral in the Senate.

for.name: 22 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Wyden, Blumenthal, Klobuchar, and Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; all 22 are Democrats.

against.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or committee vote on the bill since its June 2025 referral; the action record shows no committee activity after referral.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and no Republican senator has moved it toward floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; in a Senate run by Republicans, the bill has not advanced past committee referral.

industries.note: These firms make money collecting and selling inferences from app, location, and purchase data; the bill would ban them from collecting or disclosing reproductive and sexual health data — including inferred and location data — except as strictly necessary to serve the user, and restricts disclosure to government entities too. Their revenue from this data category would go away, which is exactly the point from the public's side.

industries.industry: Consumer health, fertility, and period-tracking apps
industries.note: These apps would have to minimize what they collect, publish detailed privacy policies, honor access and deletion requests within 15 days, and face per-day statutory damages without arbitration shields — a real cost, heaviest for small developers. But their users are the people the bill protects, so the industry's interest in keeping data practices and the public's interest in privacy pull apart here.

industries.industry: Search engines, social media platforms, and mobile carriers
industries.note: Location and search data that might indicate someone sought reproductive health services would fall under the bill's definition, so platforms could no longer collect or sell it, and could be sued for violations by users directly.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the Senate majority and chairing the Commerce Committee, and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote this Congress. Its realistic paths are dying in committee, or its text serving as a template for state laws and future Congresses, as earlier versions of the same proposal have.
